hints: Hint 1: Look closely at the three polysaccharides and ask yourself which one is straight and unbranched, and which ones have side branches.
Hint 2: Remember amylase can only cut alpha-1,4 bonds, so the more alpha-1,6 branch points a molecule has, the more bonds will be left uncut.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the structure of each polysaccharide**
All three are made of alpha-glucose, but their shapes are different. Amylose is a long unbranched chain with only $\alpha$-1,4 glycosidic bonds. Amylopectin is branched with mostly $\alpha$-1,4 bonds plus some $\alpha$-1,6 bonds at branch points. Glycogen is very highly branched with many $\alpha$-1,6 bonds.

Step 2: **Apply what amylase can do**
Amylase breaks only $\alpha$-1,4 bonds. It cannot break the $\alpha$-1,6 bonds at branch points. So a molecule with no branches can be almost fully digested, while highly branched molecules will be left with undigested limit dextrins around each branch.

Step 3: **Rank them and pick the row**
Most complete digestion: amylose (+++) because it has only $\alpha$-1,4 bonds. Next: amylopectin (++) with some branches. Least: glycogen (+) with the most branches. That pattern is exactly row D.

options.A: This reverses the logic. It gives amylose the least digestion, but amylose has no alpha-1,6 bonds so amylase can digest it most completely.
options.B: This gives glycogen the most digestion, but glycogen is the most branched so it has the most amylase-resistant alpha-1,6 bonds.
options.C: This gives amylopectin the least digestion, but amylopectin is less branched than glycogen, so it should be digested more than glycogen.
options.D: Correct. Amylose (+++) has only alpha-1,4 bonds, amylopectin (++) has some alpha-1,6 branches, and glycogen (+) has many alpha-1,6 branches that amylase cannot break.
